First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}|-(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & -3-\lambda  \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+15\lambda )+(-5-\lambda )+(5+\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+13\lambda -10 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $10:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 5,\pm 10
$$

Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}+2(1)^{2}-13(1)+10 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is a root of the equation. So, we can factor $(\lambda -1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +10$ using synthetic division:

| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-13$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $3$ | $-10$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $-10$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +5)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.$
